chmmc-2015-power-01a.title: Distribution table
chmmc-2015-power-01a.body:
The probabilities of the sums $2,3,\dots,12$ are $\frac1{36},\frac2{36},\frac3{36},\frac4{36},\frac5{36},\frac6{36},\frac5{36},\frac4{36},\frac3{36},\frac2{36},\frac1{36}$. The distribution is symmetric about $7$, so the weighted average is $7$ (direct computation: $\frac{1}{36}(2+6+12+20+30+42+40+36+30+22+12)=\frac{252}{36}=7$).

**Answer: 7**

chmmc-2015-power-01a.title: Symmetry of the die
chmmc-2015-power-01a.body:
Each die has expected value $\frac{1+2+\dots+6}6=\frac72$, and the expected value of a sum is the sum of the expected values (linearity, see the next problem): $\frac72+\frac72=7$.

**Answer: 7**

chmmc-2015-power-01b.title: Reorder the double sum
chmmc-2015-power-01b.body: All terms are nonnegative, so sums may be rearranged freely (they may be $+\infty$, in which case both sides are $+\infty$ consistently). Write $p(k,j)=\Pr(X=k\text{ and }Y=j)$. Then $$\mathbb E(X+Y)=\sum_n n\sum_{k\le n}p(k,n-k)=\sum_{k\ge1}\sum_{j\ge1}(k+j)\,p(k,j),$$ since every pair $(k,j)$ of positive integers occurs exactly once, with $n=k+j$ (for $k\ge n$ we have $n-k\le0$ and $\Pr(Y=n-k)=0$, so the restriction $k\le n$ loses nothing). Split $(k+j)p=kp+jp$: $$\mathbb E(X+Y)=\sum_k k\sum_jp(k,j)+\sum_j j\sum_kp(k,j)=\sum_kk\Pr(X=k)+\sum_jj\Pr(Y=j)=\mathbb EX+\mathbb EY,$$ because summing the joint probabilities over all values of one variable gives the probability for the other. ∎

chmmc-2015-power-01c.title: Linearity
chmmc-2015-power-01c.body:
Let $D_i$ be the outcome of the $i$th die; each has $\mathbb ED_i=\frac72$. By linearity $\mathbb E\sum_{i=1}^{10}D_i=10\cdot\frac72=35$.

**Answer: 35**

chmmc-2015-power-02a.title: A player who wins everything
chmmc-2015-power-02a.body: Let one participant $W$ win all of their games. Choose any $k$ participants including $W$ (possible since $n>k>0$). A participant who won against all of these $k$ would in particular have beaten $W$, but nobody beat $W$. So this set of $k$ has no participant who beat all of them, and the outcome is not $k$-good. ∎

chmmc-2015-power-02b.title: The cycle
chmmc-2015-power-02b.body: Let the participants be $A,B,C$ with $A$ beating $B$, $B$ beating $C$ and $C$ beating $A$ (each wins exactly one game and loses exactly one game). For $k=1$, $k$-goodness means: for every participant there is somebody who beat them. $B$ was beaten by $A$, $C$ by $B$, and $A$ by $C$. So the outcome is $1$-good. ∎

chmmc-2015-power-02c.title: Independence over the other participants
chmmc-2015-power-02c.body: Only the $n-k$ participants outside the chosen set can beat all of the $k$. Fix one of them, $A$. The $k$ games between $A$ and the chosen participants are independent fair coin flips, so $A$ beats all $k$ with probability $2^{-k}$ and fails to with probability $1-2^{-k}$. The games involving different outside participants $A,A'$ and the chosen set are disjoint sets of games, so these events are independent for the $n-k$ outside participants. Hence $P_{n,k}=(1-2^{-k})^{n-k}$.

chmmc-2015-power-02d.title: Union bound
chmmc-2015-power-02d.body: The outcome fails to be $k$-good iff for at least one of the $\binom nk$ sets $S$ of $k$ participants, no participant beat all of $S$; call such a set *bad*. Each set is bad with probability $P_{n,k}$ (the events for different sets are not independent, but we do not need that). By the union bound $$\Pr(\text{not }k\text{-good})=\Pr(S_1\text{ bad or }S_2\text{ bad or}\dots)\le\sum_i\Pr(S_i\text{ bad})=\binom nkP_{n,k}<1.$$ So $\Pr(k\text{-good})>0$. ∎

chmmc-2015-power-02e.title: From probability to existence
chmmc-2015-power-02e.body: There are $2^{\binom n2}$ possible outcomes (sequences of coin flips), all equally likely. The probability that the random outcome is $k$-good equals (number of $k$-good outcomes)$/2^{\binom n2}$, and by the previous problem it is positive. So the number of $k$-good outcomes is at least $1$: a $k$-good outcome exists. ∎

chmmc-2015-power-02f.title: Exponential beats polynomial
chmmc-2015-power-02f.body: We have $\binom nk\le n^k$ and $1-2^{-k}\le e^{-2^{-k}}$. Hence $$\binom nkP_{n,k}\le n^k\,e^{-(n-k)/2^k}=e^{k/2^k}\,n^ke^{-n/2^k}.$$ For fixed $k$ the constant $e^{k/2^k}$ is fixed, and $n^ke^{-n/2^k}\to0$ as $n\to\infty$ because an exponential grows faster than any polynomial (e.g. $\ln(n^ke^{-n/2^k})=k\ln n-n/2^k\to-\infty$). So for all large $n$, $\binom nkP_{n,k}<1$, and by the previous problems a $k$-good tournament with $n$ participants exists. ∎

chmmc-2015-power-03a.title: Two cases
chmmc-2015-power-03a.body:
*Case 1: all three pairwise distances are at least $2$.* Put a unit disk centered at each dot; disks centered at points at distance $\ge2$ have disjoint interiors.

*Case 2: some two dots $U,V$ are at distance $<2$.* A unit disk $D_1$ centered at the midpoint $O$ of $UV$ covers both ($OU=OV<1$). If the third dot $W$ is in $D_1$, one disk suffices (place the other two disks far away). Otherwise $|OW|>1$; put the second disk $D_2$ centered at the point $Z$ on ray $OW$ with $|OZ|=|OW|+1$. Then $|ZW|=1$, so $D_2$ covers $W$, and $|OZ|>2$, so $D_1$ and $D_2$ do not overlap. Place the third disk anywhere away from them. ∎

chmmc-2015-power-03b.title: Area bookkeeping
chmmc-2015-power-03b.body:
The interior angle of a regular hexagon is $120^\circ$, so each of the $6$ vertex disks meets the hexagon in a sector of area $\frac13\pi$, giving $6\cdot\frac\pi3=2\pi$; the center disk adds $\pi$. (Disks at adjacent vertices are tangent, and the vertex disks do not reach the center disk, so there is no overlap.) The covered area is $3\pi$. The hexagon consists of $6$ equilateral triangles of side $2$, each of area $\sqrt3$, so its area is $6\sqrt3$. The covered fraction is $\frac{3\pi}{6\sqrt3}=\frac{\pi}{2\sqrt3}\approx0.907$.

**Answer: $\frac{\pi}{2\sqrt3}\approx0.907$**

chmmc-2015-power-03c.title: Linearity of expectation
chmmc-2015-power-03c.body:
Let $X_i=1$ if the $i$th point $Z_i$ is covered and $0$ otherwise; the number covered is $X=\sum_{i=1}^{10}X_i$, so $\mathbb EX=\sum\Pr(Z_i\text{ covered})$ by linearity. The covering pattern is periodic under translation by the vectors between hexagon centers (a lattice $\Lambda$). Moving the grid by $P$ is equivalent to keeping the grid fixed and translating the point: $Z_i$ is covered iff $Z_i-P$ lies in the original covered set. As $P$ is uniform on the fundamental cell (the hexagon), $Z_i-P$ is uniform modulo $\Lambda$, so the probability that it lands in a disk equals the covered fraction of a hexagon, $\frac{\pi}{2\sqrt3}$ from the previous problem. Therefore $$\mathbb EX=10\cdot\frac\pi{2\sqrt3}=\frac{5\pi}{\sqrt3}\approx9.07.$$

**Answer: $\frac{5\pi}{\sqrt3}\approx9.07$**

chmmc-2015-power-03d.title: From expectation to existence
chmmc-2015-power-03d.body: Suppose every shift of the pattern covered at most $9$ of the $10$ points. Then the expected number covered would be at most $9$, contradicting $\frac{5\pi}{\sqrt3}>9$. So some shift covers all $10$ points. In that arrangement at most $10$ disks contain any of the points; keep just those disks (the pattern's disks already have disjoint interiors) and, if fewer than $10$ are used, place the remaining coins far away. This wins the game. ∎
